title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
summary: Explore a sudden severe headache and examiner expectations.

aim.text: Assess history taking in a sudden severe headache, recognising subarachnoid haemorrhage through the time-critical, red-flag approach.

candidateInstructions.text: You are the emergency doctor. Ms Sarah Khan, 38, has come in with a sudden severe headache. Observations: BP 158/94, HR 96, temperature 36.9, GCS 15. Take a focused history. Do not examine. At the end, summarise and state your initial plan.

items: Onset 14:10 at the gym: sudden, at its worst within a minute, worst headache of her life, back of the head.
Vomited twice, neck stiff and sore, light hurts. Felt woozy, no clear blackout, no fit.
No head injury, fever or rash. No weakness, speech or vision change.
No similar headaches before; occasional mild migraine.
High blood pressure on ramipril. Smokes 15 a day. No blood thinners, no cocaine, no allergies.
Mother died suddenly at 52 ("something in her head"); an uncle had polycystic kidney disease.
Concern if asked: "Is it a bleed like my mum? Am I going to die?"

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Hello, I am Dr Shah, one of the emergency doctors. Can you confirm your name and date of birth?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Sarah Khan, 3rd May 1988.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Could you tell me what has been happening, in your own words?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I was at the gym and got a sudden terrible headache at the back of my head. It is the worst I have ever had.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you. Is there anything else you have noticed?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I have been sick twice, my neck is stiff and the light hurts my eyes.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I am going to ask some specific questions now. Exactly what time did it start, and how quickly did it become severe?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: About ten past two. It was at its worst within a minute, like being hit.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Did you black out, have a fit, or feel faint?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I felt woozy but did not black out. No fit.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any head injury, fever or rash?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No, none of those.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any weakness, numbness, speech or vision problems, or double vision?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No, only light bothers me.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Have you had headaches like this before?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Never like this. I get mild migraines sometimes.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Do you take blood thinners, or use cocaine or other drugs?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No to both.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Do you have any medical conditions, take regular medicines, or have allergies?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: High blood pressure, ramipril. No allergies.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Does anyone in your family have bleeds in the brain, aneurysms or kidney problems? Do you smoke?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: My mum died suddenly at 52, they said something in her head. My uncle had polycystic kidney disease. I smoke fifteen a day.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: What do you think might be going on, and what worries you most?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Is it a bleed like my mum? Am I going to die?

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: That is an understandable fear. I will be honest: this could be bleeding around the brain, and it needs urgent tests. We are acting quickly. To summarise, you had a sudden severe headache that peaked within a minute at 14:10, with vomiting, a stiff neck and light sensitivity, you have high blood pressure and smoke, and your mother died suddenly. I am arranging an urgent CT scan of your head, bloods and a heart tracing, and I will speak to the senior doctor and the neurosurgical team. Any questions?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No. Thank you.

head: Task
Expected in this station
rows: Introduce yourself, check name and date of birth, start with an open question, listen, signpost, summarise and state a plan.

Thunderclap headache peaking within a minute at 14:10 on exertion, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, brief wooziness, hypertension, smoker, family history of sudden death and polycystic kidney disease, no blood thinners.
Exact onset time and speed, collapse, fit, head injury, fever, rash, neurological symptoms, previous headaches, blood thinners, cocaine, hypertension, smoking, family history.

Say aloud: ABCDE, glucose, urgent CT head, bloods, ECG, neurological observations, analgesia and antiemetic, senior and neurosurgical discussion, lumbar puncture or CT angiography per pathway if CT negative.
Acknowledge fear, stay calm, do not falsely reassure, say you would ask the senior when unsure.

head: Situation
Good response
rows: Recheck ABCDE and GCS, call the senior and critical care, repeat glucose, tell the neurosurgical team.
Patient vomits and has a fit
Protect the airway, call for help, follow the seizure protocol, arrange urgent CT.
Acknowledge the fear, be honest, explain what happens next.

head: Medical term
Say instead
rows: Bleeding in the space around the brain
A weak, ballooned part of a blood vessel
A quick scan that takes pictures of the brain
A needle test in the lower back to take fluid

head: Question
Model reply
rows: "It could be. The scan will show us quickly."
"This can be serious, and we are acting fast, which gives you the best chance."
"If it is a bleed from a weak vessel, a specialist team may treat it with a procedure or an operation."
"Some causes run in families. The specialist team will advise you later."

patientQuestions.text: Tips: acknowledge the feeling first, short sentences, check understanding, no false reassurance.

examinerQuestions.question: What are your immediate actions and investigations?

items: ABCDE, glucose, IV access, bloods, ECG, regular GCS and neurological observations.
Urgent non-contrast CT head, most sensitive within 6 hours of onset.
If CT is negative and more than 6 hours from onset, follow the local pathway: lumbar puncture (at least 12 hours after onset, for xanthochromia) or CT angiography.
Early senior and neurosurgical discussion, analgesia and antiemetic, nil by mouth.

examinerQuestions.question: What are the causes and risk factors?

items: Ruptured berry aneurysm is the commonest cause.
Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, family history, polycystic kidney disease, heavy alcohol, cocaine.
Other causes: arteriovenous malformation, trauma.

examinerQuestions.question: Which headache features are red flags?

items: Thunderclap onset, exertional onset, neck stiffness, vomiting, collapse or seizure.
Focal neurology, reduced GCS, fever with rash, new headache over 50, papilloedema.

examinerQuestions.question: What are the main complications and treatments?

items: Rebleeding, hydrocephalus, vasospasm with delayed ischaemia, seizures, hyponatraemia.
Nimodipine for confirmed SAH, BP control as advised by neurosurgery, and aneurysm securing by coiling or clipping.

examinerQuestionPrompts.text: Model answers are in Learning mode.

items: Not asking exactly when and how fast it began.
Calling it migraine without excluding red flags.
No CT, or no senior and neurosurgical escalation.
No summary or plan, or jargon without explanation.
Ask exactly how fast the headache peaked.
Thunderclap onset is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.
CT head is most sensitive early, so time matters.
Do not label migraine without excluding red flags.
